evidence.label: The PCP-for-PPAD conjecture: a quasilinear reduction

headline: End-of-Line puzzles turn into number circuits only slightly bigger that tolerate many broken gates, the paper claims.
scope: The result is a deterministic reduction from End-of-Line instances to generalized circuits. Its error and failure-fraction constants are fixed, and size is counted in exact binary length.
plain: PPAD is a class of search problems where a solution must exist for a parity reason. Babichenko, Papadimitriou and Rubinstein conjectured that its core puzzle can be rewritten as a number circuit only slightly longer than the input. That rewriting must still give an answer when a fixed fraction of gates are broken by an adversary. This paper claims to prove that conjecture. No Lean formalization is listed.
doesNot: This does not prove new running-time lower bounds for Nash equilibria; those still need an extra hardness assumption.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Babichenko, Papadimitriou and Rubinstein, who posed the conjecture
scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proof holds, it settles a stated conjecture that links robust checking with the complexity of equilibria.

explanation:
Think of a huge maze of one-way corridors. Each room has at most one way in and one way out. You stand in a room with an exit but no entrance. Follow the corridors and you must reach a dead end, a room with no exit. Ends come in pairs, so another end must exist. Finding one can still take an enormous number of steps.

That puzzle is End-of-Line. The rooms are bit strings, and two small circuits name each room's next and previous room. The input length N counts the full description of both circuits[12]. PPAD is the class of search problems built on this parity argument[1]. Finding a Nash equilibrium of a game is a famous member.

A generalized circuit is a second language for the same class[2]. Each wire carries a number between 0 and 1. Each gate demands a local rule, up to a small error ε[3]. Take an Add gate fed 0.3 and 0.5. Its output must sit within ε of 0.8. Fed 0.7 and 0.6, the sum caps at 1, so the output must sit within ε of 1.

In 2016, Babichenko, Papadimitriou and Rubinstein posed the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture[4]. It asks for a short rewrite of End-of-Line into such circuits. Both the numerical error and the fraction of broken gates must be fixed positive constants[4]. The broken-gate allowance is the hard part. The answer must come out even if an adversary chooses which gates fail[5]. Short means quasilinear: N times a fixed power of log N[6].

Put numbers on that. Take N equal to one million bits, so log₂ N is about 19.9. If the power of the log were 2, the circuit would be about 400 million bits long. A blowup like N² would instead be a trillion. The paper fixes some power but does not name it in its main statement.

Ordinary hardness proofs, even with constant error, do not give the short size[7]. In 2016 Rubinstein used encoded paths and a checkable proof system to show related hardness for two-player Nash equilibria. He left the conjecture open and flagged combining the pieces as a remaining question[8].

This paper claims to resolve the conjecture[9]. It gives fixed constants ε and δ and a deterministic rewrite into circuits of length N times a power of log N[10]. From any assignment that meets all but a δ fraction of gates, a solution to the maze can be recovered[11]. That holds whatever gates fail[11]. Such assignments always exist[13]. Neither tolerance shrinks as N grows[14].

The difficulty is needing two things at once: quasilinear total storage and robustness to a fixed fraction of failures[15]. The paper turns the maze into paths in a high-dimensional box, so an approximate fixed point lands on an endpoint. Each local step must be computable without reading the whole maze[16]. Rooms are stored as coded words, so a word with a few damaged symbols can still be decoded.

There is a limit to keep in view. Later papers derive lower bounds for computing equilibria from this conjecture. Those bounds also assume an extra exponential-time hypothesis. The paper's result concerns the rewrite itself, not those bounds[17].

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this paper in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked it. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the proof holds. The constants ε, δ and the power of log N are fixed but not given as small numbers. Equilibrium time bounds that use it still need an extra assumption. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A class of search problems whose solutions must exist by a parity argument about endpoints of paths.
The core PPAD puzzle: given circuits naming next and previous rooms, find an end of a path other than the start.
A network of gates whose wires carry numbers in [0, 1], each gate checking a simple rule up to error ε.
An efficient way to rewrite one problem as another, so a solution to the second gives one to the first.
At most the input length times a fixed power of its logarithm.
Probabilistically checkable proof: a format where checking a few spots reveals whether the whole is badly wrong.
